t: Four charges each equal to Q are placed at the four corners of a square and a charge q is placed at the centre of the square. If the system is in equilibrium, the value of q is:
s:
Let the side length of the square be a. The distance from a corner to the center of the square is r=a√2/2=a/√2.
For the system to be in equilibrium, the net force on each charge must be zero. The charge q at the center is in equilibrium due to symmetry. We must consider the equilibrium of one of the corner charges Q.
Consider the charge Q at one corner. The forces acting on it due to the other three corner charges Q are:
Force due to the two adjacent charges: F₁=1/4πϵ₀Q²/a² each, acting along the sides of the square. Their resultant F₁₂ acts along the diagonal and has magnitude F₁₂=√(F₁²+F₁²)=√2F₁=√21/4πϵ₀Q²/a².
Force due to the charge at the opposite corner: F₃=1/4πϵ₀Q²/((√2a)²)=1/4πϵ₀Q²/2a², acting along the diagonal.
The total repulsive force from the other three corner charges is directed outward along the diagonal:
Fᵣₑₚᵤₗₛᵢₒₙ=F₁₂+F₃=1/4πϵ₀Q²/a²√2+1/4πϵ₀Q²/2a²=1/4πϵ₀Q²/a²(√2+1/2).
For the corner charge to be in equilibrium, the force due to the center charge q must balance this repulsive force. Thus, the sum of all forces on the corner charge must be zero:
F_(center)=1/4πϵ₀Qq/((a/√2)²)=1/4πϵ₀2Qq/a².
Setting the net force to zero (Fᵣₑₚᵤₗₛᵢₒₙ+F_(center)=0):
1/4πϵ₀Q²/a²((2√2+1)/2)+1/4πϵ₀2Qq/a²=0.
Dividing the entire equation by 1/4πϵ₀Q/a²:
Q((1+2√2)/2)+2q=0
2q=−Q((1+2√2)/2)
q=−Q/4(1+2√2)
